sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

$g(x)=\dfrac{(2^{x}+2^{-x})\sqrt{\tan ^{-1}(x^{2}-x+1)}}{(7x^{2}+3x+1)^{3}}$

text: Let $⃗{a},⃗{b}$ and $⃗{c}$ be three non-zero vectors such that $⃗{b}$ and $⃗{c}$ are non-collinear. If $⃗{a}+5⃗{b}$ is collinear with $⃗{c},⃗{b}+6⃗{c}$ is collinear with $⃗{a}$ and $⃗{a}+α⃗{b}+β⃗{c}=\vec{0}$, then $α+β$ is equal to
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Collinearity gives

$⃗{a}+5⃗{b}=λ⃗{c},⃗{b}+6⃗{c}=μ⃗{a}$

Substituting $⃗{a}=λ⃗{c}-5⃗{b}$ in the second relation:

$⃗{b}+6⃗{c}=λμ⃗{c}-5μ⃗{b}\Rightarrow (1+5μ)⃗{b}+(6-λμ)⃗{c}=⃗{0}$

Since $⃗{b}$ and $⃗{c}$ are non-collinear, both coefficients are zero: $μ=-\dfrac{1}{5}$ and $λμ=6$, so $λ=-30$.

Then $⃗{a}+5⃗{b}=-30⃗{c}$, that is, $⃗{a}+5⃗{b}+30⃗{c}=⃗{0}$.

Subtracting this from $⃗{a}+α⃗{b}+β⃗{c}=⃗{0}$ gives $(α-5)⃗{b}+(β-30)⃗{c}=⃗{0}$, so $α=5$ and $β=30$.

$α+β=35$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text: If in a G.P. of 64 terms, the sum of all the terms is 7 times the sum of the odd terms of the G.P, then the common ratio of the G.P. is equal to
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let the first term be $a(\neq 0)$ and the common ratio $r$. For $r=1$ the condition reads $64a=7\times 32a$ and for $r=-1$ it reads $0=7\times 32a$, both false, so $r\neq \pm 1$.

The terms in odd positions, $a,ar^{2},ar^{4},\ldots ,ar^{62}$, are 32 terms of a G.P. with common ratio $r^{2}$, so their sum is

$S_{\text{odd}}=\dfrac{a\left [1-(r^{2})^{32}\right ]}{1-r^{2}}=\dfrac{a\left (1-r^{64}\right )}{(1-r)(1+r)}$

The sum of all 64 terms is $S=\dfrac{a\left (1-r^{64}\right )}{1-r}$.

$S=7S_{\text{odd}}$ gives $\dfrac{a\left (1-r^{64}\right )}{1-r}=\dfrac{7a\left (1-r^{64}\right )}{(1-r)(1+r)}$. Since $r\neq \pm 1$, $1-r^{64}\neq 0$, and cancelling the common factor gives $1+r=7\Rightarrow r=6$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: For $x\in \left (-\frac{π}{2},\frac{π}{2}\right )$, if $y(x)=\int \frac{\mathrm{cosec}x+\sin x}{\mathrm{cosec}x\sec x+\tan x\sin ^{2}x}dx$, and $\lim _{x\to \left (\frac{π}{2}\right )^{-}}y(x)=0$ then $y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )$ is equal to
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Writing $\mathrm{cosec}x+\sin x=\dfrac{1+\sin ^{2}x}{\sin x}$ and $\mathrm{cosec}x\sec x+\tan x\sin ^{2}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}+\dfrac{\sin ^{3}x}{\cos x}=\dfrac{1+\sin ^{4}x}{\sin x\cos x}$, the integrand becomes

$\frac{(1+\sin ^{2}x)\cos x}{1+\sin ^{4}x}.$

Putting $\sin x=t$, $\cos x\qquad dx=dt$, and dividing numerator and denominator by $t^{2}$:

$y=\int \frac{1+t^{2}}{1+t^{4}}dt=\int \frac{1+\dfrac{1}{t^{2}}}{\left (t-\dfrac{1}{t}\right )^{2}+2}dt.$

With $u=t-\dfrac{1}{t}$, $du=\left (1+\dfrac{1}{t^{2}}\right )dt$:

$y=\int \frac{du}{u^{2}+2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{t-\frac{1}{t}}{\sqrt{2}}\right )+C.$

As $x\to \left (\dfrac{π}{2}\right )^{-}$, $t\to 1$ and $t-\dfrac{1}{t}\to 0$, so the limit condition gives $C=0$.

At $x=\dfrac{π}{4}$, $t=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $t-\dfrac{1}{t}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so the argument is $-\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\tan ^{-1}\left (-\frac{1}{2}\right ).$

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: Let $\mathrm{A}$ be a square matrix such that $\mathrm{AA}^{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{I}$. Then $\frac{1}{2}A\left [\left (A+A^{T}\right )^{2}+\left (A-A^{T}\right )^{2}\right ]$ is equal to
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since $A$ is a square matrix with $AA^{T}=I$, $A^{T}=A^{-1}$, so $A^{T}A=I$ as well.

Expanding both squares,

$(A+A^{T})^{2}=A^{2}+AA^{T}+A^{T}A+(A^{T})^{2},(A-A^{T})^{2}=A^{2}-AA^{T}-A^{T}A+(A^{T})^{2}$

Adding, $(A+A^{T})^{2}+(A-A^{T})^{2}=2A^{2}+2(A^{T})^{2}$.

$\frac{1}{2}A\left [2A^{2}+2(A^{T})^{2}\right ]=A^{3}+A(A^{T})^{2}=A^{3}+(AA^{T})A^{T}=A^{3}+A^{T}$

Only one factor $A^{T}$ cancels with $A$, so $A(A^{T})^{2}$ is $A^{T}$, not $I$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: If $z=\frac{1}{2}-2i$ is such that $|z+1|=αz+β(1+i),i=\sqrt{-1}$ and $α,β\in \mathrm{ℝ}$, then $α+β$ is equal to
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To begin with, let's analyze the given equation:

$|z+1|=αz+β(1+i)$

First, we compute the modulus of the left side:

Let's take the given value of z,

$z=\frac{1}{2}-2i$

Now, we find $z+1$:

$z+1=\left (\frac{1}{2}-2i\right )+1=\frac{3}{2}-2i$

Then, the modulus of $z+1$ is calculated as follows:

$|z+1|=\left |\frac{3}{2}-2i\right |=\sqrt{\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{2}+(-2)^{2}}$

$|z+1|=\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+4}$

$|z+1|=\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{16}{4}}$

$|z+1|=\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}}$

$|z+1|=\frac{5}{2}$

Now we need to equate the modulus to the right-hand side of the equation and solve for $α$ and $β$. Let's rewrite the equation:

$\frac{5}{2}=αz+β(1+i)$

Substitute $z$ with its value:

$\frac{5}{2}=α\left (\frac{1}{2}-2i\right )+β(1+i)$

Rewrite the equation separating real and imaginary parts:

$\frac{5}{2}=α\left (\frac{1}{2}\right )-2αi+β+βi$

$\frac{5}{2}=\left (α\frac{1}{2}+β\right )+(-2α+β)i$

For the above equality to hold, both real and imaginary parts must be equal.

Equating real parts:

$α\frac{1}{2}+β=\frac{5}{2}$

Equating imaginary parts:

$-2α+β=0$

We now have a system of two linear equations:

1) $\frac{α}{2}+β=\frac{5}{2}$

2) $-2α+β=0$

Let's solve the system by isolating $β$ from the second equation and then substituting it into the first one:

$β=2α$

Now substitute $β$ in the first equation:

$\frac{α}{2}+2α=\frac{5}{2}$

$α\left (\frac{1}{2}+2\right )=\frac{5}{2}$

$α\left (\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{2}\right )=\frac{5}{2}$

$α\left (\frac{5}{2}\right )=\frac{5}{2}$

To find the value of $α$, we divide both sides by $\frac{5}{2}$:

$α=1$

Now, we use the value of $α$ to find $β$:

$β=2α$

$β=2\cdot 1$

$β=2$

Finally, we add both $α$ and $β$ to find $α+β$:

$α+β=1+2=3$

The value of $α+β$ is 3.

So, the correct answer is Option C) 3.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: Let $PQR$ be a triangle with $R(-1,4,2)$. Suppose $M(2,1,2)$ is the mid point of $\mathrm{PQ}$. The distance of the centroid of $△\mathrm{PQR}$ from the point of intersection of the lines $\frac{x-2}{0}=\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z+3}{-1}$ and $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+3}{-3}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The centroid G lies on the median RM with $RG:GM=2:1$:

$G=\frac{R+2M}{3}=\left (\frac{-1+4}{3},\frac{4+2}{3},\frac{2+4}{3}\right )=(1,2,2)$

On the first line the denominator under $x-2$ is 0, so $x=2$ throughout; its general point is $(2,2s,-3-s)$. The general point of the second line is $(1+t,-3-3t,-1+t)$.

Equating x-coordinates, $1+t=2\Rightarrow t=1$, giving $(2,-6,0)$ on the second line. On the first line $2s=-6\Rightarrow s=-3$ and $z=-3-(-3)=0$, which agrees. So the lines meet at $A(2,-6,0)$.

$AG=\sqrt{(2-1)^{2}+(-6-2)^{2}+(0-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{1+64+4}=\sqrt{69}$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: A line with direction ratios $2,1,2$ meets the lines $x=y+2=z$ and $x+2=2y=2z$ respectively at the points $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{Q}$. If the length of the perpendicular from the point $(1,2,12)$ to the line $\mathrm{PQ}$ is $l$, then $l^{2}$ is $__________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{t},\mathrm{t}-2,\mathrm{t})$ and $\mathrm{Q}(2\mathrm{s}-2,\mathrm{s},\mathrm{s})$

D.R's of PQ are 2, 1, 2

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{2\mathrm{s}-2-\mathrm{t}}{2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{s}-\mathrm{t}+2}{1}=\dfrac{\mathrm{s}-\mathrm{t}}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=6\text{and}\mathrm{s}=2 \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}(6,4,6)\text{and}\mathrm{Q}(2,2,2) \\ \mathrm{PQ}:\dfrac{\mathrm{x}-2}{2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{y}-2}{1}=\dfrac{\mathrm{z}-2}{2}=λ \end{array}$

Let $\mathrm{F}(2λ+2,λ+2,2λ+2)$

$\mathrm{A}(1,2,12)$

$\mathrm{AF}\leftarrow \cdot \mathrm{PQ}\leftarrow =0$

$\therefore λ=2$

So $F(6,4,6)$ and $AF=\sqrt{65}$

text: If the points of intersection of two distinct conics $x^{2}+y^{2}=4b$ and $\frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ lie on the curve $y^{2}=3x^{2}$, then $3\sqrt{3}$ times the area of the rectangle formed by the intersection points is $_________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Putting $y^{2}=3x^{2}$ in both the conics

We get $x^{2}=b$ and $\frac{b}{16}+\frac{3}{b}=1$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{b}=4,12(\mathrm{b}=4$ is rejected because curves coincide)

$\therefore \mathrm{b}=12$

Hence points of intersection are

$(\pm \sqrt{12},\pm 6)\Rightarrow \text{area of rectangle}=432$

text: Let $f(x)=2^{x}-x^{2},x\in \mathrm{ℝ}$. If $m$ and $n$ are respectively the number of points at which the curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=f^{'}(x)$ intersect the $x$-axis, then the value of $\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{n}$ is $___________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$f(x)=2^{x}-x^{2},f^{'}(x)=2^{x}\ln 2-2x,f^{''}(x)=2^{x}(\ln 2)^{2}-2$

$f^{''}$ is strictly increasing and takes negative and positive values, so it has exactly one zero. Hence $f^{'}$ first decreases and then increases, so $f^{'}$ has at most two zeros, and $f$ (monotonic on at most three intervals) has at most three zeros.

Zeros of $f$: $f(2)=4-4=0$ and $f(4)=16-16=0$; also $f(-1)=\dfrac{1}{2}-1<0$ and $f(0)=1>0$, so there is one zero in $(-1,0)$. So $y=f(x)$ meets the $x$-axis at exactly three points: $m=3$.

Zeros of $f^{'}$: $f^{'}(0)=\ln 2>0$, $f^{'}(1)=2\ln 2-2<0$ and $f^{'}(4)=16\ln 2-8>0$, so $f^{'}$ has a zero in $(0,1)$ and one in $(1,4)$. With at most two zeros, $y=f^{'}(x)$ meets the $x$-axis at exactly two points: $n=2$.

$m+n=3+2=5$

Hence, the answer is 5.

text: If the solution curve $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $\left (1+y^{2}\right )(1+\log _{\mathrm{e}}x)dx+xdy=0,x>0$ passes through the point $(1,1)$ and $y(e)=\frac{α-\tan \left (\frac{3}{2}\right )}{β+\tan \left (\frac{3}{2}\right )}$, then $α+2β$ is $_________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} \int \left (\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right )dx+\int \dfrac{dy}{1+y^{2}}=0 \\ \ln x+\dfrac{(\ln x)^{2}}{2}+\tan ^{-1}y=C \end{array}$

Put $x=y=1$

$\begin{array}{l} \therefore C=\dfrac{π}{4} \\ \Rightarrow \ln x+\dfrac{(\ln x)^{2}}{2}+\tan ^{-1}y=\dfrac{π}{4} \end{array}$

Put $x=e$

$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \mathrm{y}=\tan \left (\dfrac{π}{4}-\dfrac{3}{2}\right )=\dfrac{1-\tan \frac{3}{2}}{1+\tan \frac{3}{2}} \\ \therefore α=1,β=1 \\ \Rightarrow α+2β=3 \end{array}$
